12.01.title: Exact viscous solutions
12.01.html:
The Navier-Stokes equations rarely have exact solutions, but a handful exist, and they teach a lot. When the flow is parallel, the nonlinear convection term vanishes and the equations become linear. Phase 11 solved two steady cases, Couette and Poiseuille flow. This lesson adds a time-dependent one: a plate suddenly set in motion. It shows how viscosity spreads momentum, and why the layer it affects grows as νt​.

Parallel flows

Take u=(u(y,t),0,0). Continuity, ∂u/∂x=0, holds automatically, and (u⋅∇)u=u∂u/∂x=0. The x-momentum equation reduces to

∂t∂u​=−ρ1​∂x∂p​+ν∂y2∂2u​.
  • Steady, no pressure gradient, moving top wall: Couette, a linear profile.
  • Steady, constant pressure gradient, fixed walls: Poiseuille, a parabola.
  • Unsteady, no pressure gradient: a diffusion equation for momentum, with ν as the diffusivity.

Stokes' first problem

Fluid lies at rest above a plate that is suddenly set moving at speed U at t=0. The boundary conditions are u(0,t)=U and u→0 far away. There’s no length scale in the problem except νt​, so the solution must depend only on η=y/(2νt​). The PDE becomes an ODE, u′′+2ηu′=0, with the solution

Uu​=erfc(2νt​y​).

The velocity falls to 1% of U where erfc(η)=0.01, at η=1.8214. So the layer of moving fluid is

δ99​=3.643νt​.

Four times the time gives twice the thickness. The wall shear stress is τw​=μU/πνt​: large at first, then dying away as the gradient spreads out. The same νt​ law sets the thickness of boundary layers (lesson 12.03) and, with thermal diffusivity in place of ν, how deep heat soaks into a wall.

Worked exampleWater above a jerked plate

Water (ν=10−6 m²/s) above a plate set moving at 0.5 m/s. Explicit finite differences on 400 cells over 6 cm, compared with the erfc solution:

  1. At t = 2.5, 10 and 40 s the largest error is 2.3×10−4, 5.8×10−5 and 1.4×10−5 m/s.
  2. The 99% layer is 5.759, 11.519 and 23.039 mm, against 3.643νt​ = 5.760, 11.520 and 23.040 mm.
  3. Each fourfold increase in time doubles the layer: ratios 2.0000 and 2.0001.
  4. Wall shear at 10 s: τw​=10−3⋅0.5/π⋅10−5​=0.0892 Pa.

Exercise 1Honey on a spoon

Honey has ν≈7×10−3 m²/s. How thick is the moving layer 1 s and 10 s after a plate starts moving under it? How long does water take to build a layer of the same thickness as honey does in 1 s?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. δ99​(1 s)=3.6437×10−3​=0.3048 m.
  2. δ99​(10 s)=3.6437×10−2​=0.9638 m: the whole jar moves almost at once.
  3. Water needs νt equal: t=7×10−3/10−6=7000 s, nearly 2 hours.

quiz.q: 99% layer thickness (mm) in water (ν = 1e-6 m²/s) after 25 s. 3 decimals.
Wall shear (Pa) 4 s after a plate starts at 1 m/s under water (μ = 1e-3, ν = 1e-6). 4 decimals.
By what factor does the layer grow when the time increases ninefold?
In a parallel flow u(y, t), the convective term (u·∇)u is:
quiz.explain: u ∂u/∂x = 0 because u doesn’t vary along x.

quiz.q: In Stokes' first problem the velocity profile is:
quiz.explain: A similarity solution of the diffusion equation.

12.02.title: Low-Reynolds flow
12.02.html:
Below the Limmat’s surface, fine silt can stay suspended for hours. Bacteria swim, pollen drifts and fog droplets hang in the air. At these tiny scales the Reynolds number is far below 1: viscosity overwhelms inertia. This world, called creeping flow or Stokes flow, behaves very differently from ours. Flow is perfectly reversible, there’s no coasting, and drag is proportional to speed, not speed squared.

Stokes flow

When Re=ρUL/μ≪1, drop the inertia terms from Navier-Stokes:

∇p=μ∇2u,∇⋅u=0.

These equations are linear and have no time derivative. Reverse the motion of the boundaries and the flow retraces itself exactly. That’s why a scallop opening and closing its shell can’t swim at low Re (Purcell’s scallop theorem), and why bacteria rotate corkscrew flagella instead.

Stokes drag on a sphere

Stokes solved the flow around a sphere of radius R moving at speed U. Integrating the pressure and viscous stresses over its surface gives

F=6πμRU,

one third from pressure and two thirds from friction. In terms of a drag coefficient, CD​=24/Re with Re based on the diameter.

Settling velocity

A grain sinks at constant speed when drag balances its weight minus buoyancy:

6πμRU=(ρp​−ρ)g34​πR3⟹U=18μ(ρp​−ρ)gd2​.

The speed goes as d2: a grain ten times smaller sinks a hundred times slower. Stokes' law holds for Re≲0.5. For bigger grains inertia adds drag; a common correlation is Schiller-Naumann, CD​=Re24​(1+0.15Re0.687), valid up to Re≈800.

Worked exampleSediment in the Limmat

Quartz grains (ρp​=2650 kg/m³) in water at 20 °C (μ=10−3 Pa s).

Diameter Stokes, mm/s With drag correlation, mm/s Re
2 µm (clay) 0.0036 0.0036 7×10−6
20 µm (silt) 0.3597 0.3579 0.0072
60 µm 3.2373 3.0916 0.19
200 µm (fine sand) 35.970 24.796 5.0
1 mm (sand) 899.25 155.10 155

At low Re the two agree within 0.5%. A 20 µm silt grain takes 2.32 h to sink through 3 m of still water; a 2 µm clay particle needs 9.7 days, which is why glacier rivers stay milky.

Exercise 1A fog droplet

A water droplet 10 µm across falls through air (μ=1.8×10−5 Pa s, ρ=1.2 kg/m³). Find its terminal speed, check the Reynolds number, and estimate how long it takes to fall 100 m.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. U=(1000−1.2)⋅9.81⋅(10−5)2/(18⋅1.8×10−5)=3.024×10−3 m/s, about 3 mm/s.
  2. Re=1.2⋅3.024×10−3⋅10−5/1.8×10−5=0.0020: deep in the Stokes regime.
  3. Falling 100 m takes 100/3.024×10−3=33069 s, about 9.2 h. Any updraft keeps fog aloft.

quiz.q: Stokes drag (µN) on a 1 mm radius sphere moving at 1 mm/s in glycerol (μ = 1.4 Pa s). 2 decimals.
Settling speed (mm/s) of a 40 µm quartz grain in water (μ = 1e-3). 4 decimals.
How many times slower does a grain settle if its diameter is 5 times smaller?
At very low Reynolds number, a swimmer that simply reverses one stroke:
options: Gets nowhere: Stokes flow is reversible

quiz.q: Stokes' law begins to overestimate the settling speed when:
quiz.explain: Inertia adds drag at higher Re.

12.03.title: Boundary layers
12.03.html:
In 1904 Ludwig Prandtl solved a puzzle that had stalled fluid mechanics. Ideal-flow theory predicted zero drag, but every real body has drag. Prandtl’s answer: viscosity matters only in a thin boundary layer next to the surface, where the velocity climbs from zero at the wall to the outer flow speed. Outside it, the flow is effectively inviscid. Splitting the problem in two made aerodynamics possible.

How thick is the layer?

Momentum diffuses away from the wall a distance νt​ in time t (lesson 12.01). Fluid travelling at U reaches position x after t=x/U, so

δ∼Uνx​​=Rex​​x​,Rex​=νUx​.

At high Re the layer is thin compared with the body, which justifies Prandtl’s simplifications: the pressure is set by the outer flow and doesn’t vary across the layer, and diffusion along x is negligible compared with diffusion across it.

The Blasius solution

For a flat plate with no pressure gradient, the boundary-layer equations have a similarity solution. With η=yU/(νx)​ and u/U=f′(η), they reduce to the Blasius equation

f′′′+21​ff′′=0,f(0)=f′(0)=0,f′(∞)=1.

It’s a boundary-value problem: we don’t know f′′(0). Shooting guesses it, integrates outwards with RK4, and adjusts the guess until f′ tends to 1. The answer, f′′(0)=0.332057, gives everything engineers need:

xδ99​​=Rex​​4.91​,Cf​=21​ρU2τw​​=Rex​​0.664​,CD​=ReL​​1.328​.

The layer stays laminar up to about Rex​≈5×105; beyond that it usually turns turbulent and thickens much faster.

Worked exampleAir over a flat plate

  1. Shooting with RK4 out to η=10 and bisection on the wall curvature gives f′′(0)=0.332057. The velocity reaches 99% of U at η=4.910, and the displacement thickness is at η=1.7208.
  2. For air at 5 m/s (ν=1.5×10−5 m²/s):
x, m Rex​ δ99​, mm Cf​
0.1 3.33×104 2.689 0.003638
0.5 1.67×105 6.013 0.001627
1.0 3.33×105 8.504 0.001150
  1. The friction drag on one side of a 1 m × 1 m plate: CD​=1.328/3.33×105​=0.002300, so F=21​⋅1.2⋅52⋅0.0023=0.03450 N.

Exercise 1A kite’s skin

A kite panel 0.6 m long flies in a 6 m/s wind over Sanur beach (ν=1.6×10−5 m²/s). Find Re at the trailing edge, the boundary-layer thickness there, and the friction coefficient. Is the layer laminar?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ReL​=6⋅0.6/1.6×10−5=225000.
  2. δ99​=4.91⋅0.6/225000​=6.211 mm.
  3. Cf​=0.664/225000​=0.001400 at the trailing edge; the average over the panel is CD​=1.328/474.3=0.002800.
  4. ReL​<5×105, so a smooth panel stays laminar (in practice, fabric seams and gusts may trip it).

quiz.q: Blasius 99% thickness (mm) at Re_x = 225000, x = 0.6 m. 3 decimals.
Local skin-friction coefficient at Re_x = 1e5. 4 decimals.
Friction drag (N) on both sides of a 0.5 m × 0.5 m plate in water at 0.4 m/s (ν = 1e-6, ρ = 1000). 4 decimals.
Blasius' equation is solved by shooting because:
options: One wall condition, f''(0), is unknown and must be found from the condition at infinity

12.04.title: Separation
12.04.html:
Watch a river flow past a boulder. Upstream the water hugs the rock; behind it, the flow breaks away into a swirling, slack wake where leaves circle. That break-away is separation, and it decides most of the drag on blunt bodies. It happens because the boundary layer, already slowed by friction, can’t push uphill against rising pressure.

The adverse pressure gradient

Outside the boundary layer, Bernoulli links pressure and speed: where the outer flow Ue​(x) speeds up, pressure falls (a favourable gradient); where it slows down, pressure rises (an adverse gradient). Across the thin layer the pressure is the same as outside, so the slow fluid near the wall feels the same push. At the wall itself the momentum equation gives

μ∂y2∂2u​​wall​=dxdp​.

With dp/dx>0 the profile curves the wrong way near the wall, develops an inflection point, and eventually the wall shear τw​=μ∂u/∂y falls to zero. Beyond that point the near-wall fluid flows backwards and the layer lifts off: separation.

Thwaites' method

Integrating the boundary-layer equations across the layer gives the momentum integral equation. Thwaites noticed that, for laminar layers, it can be solved almost exactly in closed form:

θ2(x)=Ue6​0.45ν​∫0x​Ue5​dx′,λ=νθ2​dxdUe​​.

θ is the momentum thickness and λ a pressure-gradient parameter. The layer separates when λ≈−0.09. All you need is the outer velocity Ue​(x), and the result doesn’t depend on the Reynolds number: ν cancels out of λ.

The cylinder

With the ideal-flow outer velocity Ue​=2Usinθ, Thwaites predicts separation at 103.1°. The exact laminar boundary-layer solution for this velocity gives 104.5°, and Pohlhausen’s older method 109.5°, so the literature range is 104–110° and Thwaites lands 1.4° below the exact value. In real flows separation happens much earlier, near 80°, because the wake itself changes the pressure field. Feeding Thwaites the measured pressures (Hiemenz’s fit) reproduces that.

Worked exampleWhere the flow leaves the cylinder

  1. At the front stagnation point λ=0.0750 (Thwaites' exact limit). At 60°, λ=0.0589; past 90° the gradient turns adverse, and at 120° λ=−0.5100.
  2. With Ue​=2Usinθ on 200 001 points, λ reaches −0.09 at 103.11°, 1.4° short of the exact 104.5°.
  3. A cylinder of a different size, speed and fluid (R = 0.2 m, 7 m/s, ν=1.5×10−5) gives the same angle to 10−6 degrees: Re drops out.
  4. With the Hiemenz fit to measured pressures, separation moves to 78.62°, close to the 80° seen in experiments.
  5. For a boulder 0.3 m across in a 1 m/s river, the momentum thickness at 90° is only 0.1342 mm.

Exercise 1Is the layer still attached?

On an ideal-flow cylinder, λ=0.45cosθ∫0θ​sin5tdt/sin6θ. With ∫0θ​sin5tdt=158​−cosθ+32​cos3θ−51​cos5θ, evaluate λ at 100°. Is the layer attached there?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. cos100°=−0.17365, sin100°=0.98481.
  2. The integral: 0.53333+0.17365−0.00349+0.00003=0.70352.
  3. λ=0.45⋅(−0.17365)⋅0.70352/0.984816=−0.05497/0.91224=−0.06026.
  4. −0.06026>−0.09: adverse, but the layer is still attached. It separates about 3° further on.

quiz.q: Thwaites λ at 100° on an ideal-flow cylinder (integral 0.70352). 5 decimals.
Momentum thickness (mm) at a stagnation point where dUe/dx = 20 1/s in water (ν = 1e-6). 5 decimals.
Thwaites' value of λ at separation.
Separation is caused by:
quiz.explain: Rising pressure stops the slowed layer.
options: An adverse pressure gradient acting on slow near-wall fluid

12.05.title: Drag
12.05.html:
A cyclist riding along the Zürichsee at 35 km/h spends most of their effort pushing air aside. Drag on a body comes in two kinds, and which one dominates depends on the shape. For a rider, almost all of it is pressure drag from the separated wake, and that’s why tucking into a lower position is worth so much.

Friction and pressure drag

The force of the fluid on a body has two parts. Friction drag is the wall shear stress integrated over the surface; it dominates on streamlined bodies such as a thin plate, a fish or a glider wing. Pressure drag (form drag) comes from the low pressure in the separated wake behind the body; it dominates on bluff bodies such as cylinders, cars and cyclists. Both are lumped into a drag coefficient,

FD​=21​ρU2CD​A.

A flat plate side-on to the flow has CD​≈0.003 (friction only); a cylinder has CD​≈1.2; a plate facing the flow, ≈2. For people and bikes, CD​ and the frontal area A are hard to separate, so they are measured together as CD​A, in m².

Power and the v³ law

Power is force times speed. In still air the aerodynamic part is

Paero​=21​ρCD​Av3,

so doubling your speed needs eight times the aerodynamic power. Add rolling resistance Crr​mgv (linear in speed) and divide by the drivetrain efficiency. With a headwind w the drag uses the air speed v+w, but the power still uses your ground speed v: P=21​ρCD​A(v+w)2v.

Worked exampleA ride around Zürich

Air at 96.6 kPa and 15 °C: ρ=1.1679 kg/m³. An 80 kg rider and bike, Crr​=0.004, drivetrain efficiency 97%.

  1. At 200 W: upright (CD​A=0.50 m²) 29.94 km/h; on the hoods (0.32) 34.46 km/h; in the drops (0.28) 35.94 km/h; time-trial position (0.22) 38.75 km/h.
  2. Aero power on the hoods at 8 m/s is 98.63 W; at 16 m/s it’s 789.06 W. The ratio is 8.0000: the v3 law.
  3. Riding 36 km/h on the hoods takes 225.0 W: 192.6 W against the air (86%) and 32.4 W rolling.
  4. Into a 5 m/s Bise headwind, the same 200 W gives only 24.22 km/h.

Exercise 1A tailwind home

The same rider on the hoods (CD​A=0.32, ρ=1.1679) rides home at 40 km/h with a 3 m/s tailwind. Find the aerodynamic power at the wheel (before drivetrain losses) and compare it with still air.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. v=11.111 m/s; air speed v−3=8.111 m/s.
  2. P=21​⋅1.1679⋅0.32⋅8.1112⋅11.111=136.6 W.
  3. Still air: 21​⋅1.1679⋅0.32⋅11.1113=256.3 W. The tailwind almost halves the aerodynamic effort.

quiz.q: Drag force (N) at 10 m/s with C_D A = 0.32 m², ρ = 1.1679. 3 decimals.
Aero power (W) with a 3 m/s tailwind at 11.111 m/s ground speed (C_D A 0.32, ρ 1.1679). 1 decimal.
By what factor does aerodynamic power rise if speed rises 20%? 3 decimals.
For a cyclist, the dominant drag is:
quiz.explain: A bluff body with a large separated wake.

quiz.q: A thin plate aligned with the flow has drag that is mainly:
quiz.explain: No wake to speak of; only wall shear.

12.06.title: Lift and airfoils
12.06.html:
A kite tugging on its line over Sanur beach and an airliner wing work the same way. A popular myth says the air over the top must “catch up” with the air underneath, so it goes faster. It doesn’t: in reality the upper flow arrives at the trailing edge well before the lower flow. The real explanation is circulation, set by a sharp trailing edge, and the Kutta-Joukowski theorem from lesson 11.16.

The Kutta condition

Potential flow around an airfoil has a solution for every value of circulation Γ. Most of them whip the flow around the sharp trailing edge at infinite speed, which a viscous fluid won’t tolerate. When a wing starts moving, a starting vortex is shed from the trailing edge, and by Kelvin’s theorem an equal and opposite circulation stays bound to the wing. It settles at the one value for which the flow leaves the trailing edge smoothly: the Kutta condition. Then L′=ρUΓ.

Thin airfoil theory

Model the airfoil as its camber line z(x), with a sheet of vortices along it. Requiring the camber line to be a streamline at angle of attack α, and substituting x=2c​(1−cosθ), the vortex strength becomes a Fourier series with coefficients

A0​=α−π1​∫0π​dxdz​dθ,An​=π2​∫0π​dxdz​cosnθdθ.

The lift and the moment about the quarter chord follow:

CL​=π(2A0​+A1​)=2π(α−αL0​),Cm,c/4​=4π​(A2​−A1​).

The lift slope is 2π per radian (0.110 per degree) for every thin airfoil. Camber shifts the zero-lift angle αL0​ to a negative value, so a cambered wing lifts even at α=0. The theory holds until stall, typically 12–16°, when the flow separates from the upper surface.

Worked exampleThe NACA 2412

  1. A flat plate at 4°: CL​=0.43865=2πα, and the quarter-chord moment is zero.
  2. NACA 2412 (2% camber at 40% chord), Glauert integrals with 200 000 midpoints: lift slope 6.283185 per radian =2π; zero-lift angle −2.077°; Cm,c/4​=−0.0531. These match wind-tunnel values closely below stall.
  3. CL​ = 0.2278 at 0°, 0.6664 at 4°, 1.1051 at 8°.
  4. A 2.5 m² kite with this section at 6° in an 8 m/s wind (ρ=1.16 kg/m³): L=21​ρU2SCL​=82.2 N. That’s a 2D estimate; a real kite of low aspect ratio gives much less (lesson 12.07 and beyond).

Exercise 1Landing lift

A light aircraft with NACA 2412 wings (αL0​=−2.077°) lands at 30 m/s with 16 m² of wing, sea-level air (ρ=1.225). In 2D theory, what angle of attack gives a lift of 9000 N?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Required CL​=9000/(21​⋅1.225⋅302⋅16)=9000/8820=1.0204.
  2. α−αL0​=1.0204/(2π)=0.16240 rad =9.305°.
  3. α=9.305−2.077=7.23°. A real finite wing needs a few degrees more because of its tip vortices.

quiz.q: Lift coefficient of a flat plate at 5° by thin airfoil theory. 4 decimals.
C_L of an airfoil with α_L0 = −2.077° at α = 3°. 4 decimals.
Angle of attack (°) for C_L = 1.0204 with α_L0 = −2.077°. 2 decimals.

options: The flow leaves the sharp trailing edge smoothly
Upper and lower parcels meet at the trailing edge

options: Shifts the zero-lift angle negative, keeping the slope 2π
